title: Polygons & Quadrilaterals
description: Derive and apply the polygon interior angle sum formula, explore the quadrilateral hierarchy (parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus, square), and apply properties of trapezoids and kites.
goals: Find the sum of interior and exterior angles of any polygon using (n-2)·180°
Identify and apply properties of parallelograms, rectangles, rhombi, and squares
Use properties of quadrilaterals to write proofs
Apply properties of trapezoids and kites
instructionalStrategy: Derive the polygon angle sum formula by triangulating from one vertex—students see why (n-2) works.
Build the quadrilateral hierarchy as a family tree: quadrilateral → parallelogram → rectangle/rhombus → square.
Every property of a parent in the hierarchy is inherited by children—a square has ALL properties of a parallelogram, rectangle, AND rhombus.
Use coordinate geometry to verify quadrilateral properties (slopes for parallel sides, distance for congruent sides).

scaffold.title: Polygon Interior and Exterior Angle Sums
scaffold.content:
The **Polygon Interior Angle Sum Theorem** gives us a formula for the total degrees inside any convex polygon:

**Sum of interior angles = (n - 2) × 180°**

where n = number of sides.

**Why does this work?** From one vertex, you can draw diagonals to create (n - 2) triangles. Each triangle has 180°, so the total is (n - 2) × 180°.

Examples:
• Triangle (n=3): (3-2) × 180° = 180°
• Quadrilateral (n=4): (4-2) × 180° = 360°
• Pentagon (n=5): (5-2) × 180° = 540°
• Hexagon (n=6): (6-2) × 180° = 720°

For a **regular polygon** (all sides and angles equal), each angle = (n-2) × 180° / n.

**Exterior Angle Sum:** The sum of exterior angles of ANY convex polygon is always **360°**. For a regular polygon, each exterior angle = 360° / n.
scaffold.initialPrompt: A stop sign is a regular octagon (8 sides). Can you calculate the sum of its interior angles and the measure of each individual angle?

scaffold.title: I-Do: Polygon Angle Calculations

examples.problem: Find the sum of interior angles of a decagon (10 sides) and the measure of each interior angle if it is regular.
examples.solution:
Sum of interior angles: (n-2) × 180° = (10-2) × 180° = 8 × 180° = **1440°**

Each angle of a regular decagon: 1440° ÷ 10 = **144°**

Exterior angle at each vertex: 180° - 144° = 36°. Check: 36° × 10 = 360° ✓

examples.problem: The interior angles of a polygon sum to 2340°. How many sides does the polygon have?
Each interior angle of a regular polygon measures 150°. Find the number of sides and the sum of all interior angles.
examples.solution:
Each exterior angle = 180° - 150° = 30°
n = 360° ÷ 30° = **12 sides** (a regular dodecagon)

Sum = (12-2) × 180° = 10 × 180° = **1800°**
Verify: 1800° ÷ 12 = 150° per angle ✓

scaffold.initialPrompt: The exterior angles always sum to 360°, no matter how many sides. Why do you think that's true? Think about walking around the outside of the shape.

scaffold.title: We-Do: Polygon Angle Problems

problems.question: The interior angles of a polygon sum to 900°. How many sides does it have?
hints: Use the formula backwards: (n-2) × 180 = 900.
n - 2 = 900 ÷ 180 = 5. So n = 7 (a heptagon).

problems.question: Each interior angle of a regular polygon measures 156°. How many sides does it have?
hints: Each exterior angle = 180° - 156° = 24°.
Since exterior angles sum to 360°: n = 360° ÷ 24° = 15 sides.

problems.question: A convex hexagon has five angles measuring 110°, 130°, 120°, 115°, and 140°. Find the sixth angle.
hints: Sum of hexagon interior angles = (6-2) × 180° = 720°.
Sum of known angles = 110 + 130 + 120 + 115 + 140 = 615°. Missing angle = 720 - 615 = 105°.

scaffold.title: The Quadrilateral Family Hierarchy
scaffold.content:
**The Quadrilateral Family** (each type inherits all properties of its parent):

**Parallelogram** — both pairs of opposite sides parallel:
• Opposite sides are congruent
• Opposite angles are congruent
• Consecutive angles are supplementary
• Diagonals bisect each other

**Rectangle** — parallelogram with 4 right angles:
• All parallelogram properties PLUS
• Diagonals are congruent

**Rhombus** — parallelogram with 4 congruent sides:
• All parallelogram properties PLUS
• Diagonals are perpendicular
• Diagonals bisect the angles

**Square** — a rectangle AND a rhombus:
• ALL properties of parallelogram, rectangle, AND rhombus
scaffold.initialPrompt: Is every square a rectangle? Is every rectangle a square? Explain the difference.

scaffold.title: I-Do: Quadrilateral Property Applications

examples.problem: In parallelogram ABCD, ∠A = (3x + 10)° and ∠B = (5x - 30)°. Find all four angles.
In rectangle EFGH, the diagonals intersect at M. If EG = 26, find EM, MG, and FH.
examples.solution:
Rectangle diagonals bisect each other:
EM = MG = 26 ÷ 2 = **13**

Rectangle diagonals are congruent:
FH = EG = **26**

So FM = MH = 13 as well.

examples.problem: Rhombus JKLM has ∠J = 60° and each side = 10. Find all angles and both diagonal lengths.
examples.solution:
Opposite angles: ∠L = ∠J = **60°**. Consecutive supplementary: ∠K = ∠M = **120°**.

Diagonals bisect angles and are perpendicular. Let O be the intersection.
In right triangle JOK: ∠OJK = 60°/2 = 30°, JK = 10 (hypotenuse of the right triangle at O).

This is a 30-60-90 triangle:
JO = 10 × cos(30°) = 10 × (√3/2) = 5√3
KO = 10 × sin(30°) = 10 × (1/2) = 5

Diagonals: JL = 2 × 5√3 = **10√3 ≈ 17.3**, KM = 2 × 5 = **10**
Verify: (5√3)² + 5² = 75 + 25 = 100 = 10² ✓

scaffold.title: We-Do: Quadrilateral Properties

problems.question: In rhombus PQRS, the diagonals intersect at point T. If PR = 24 and QS = 10, find the length of each side of the rhombus.
hints: Diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other AND are perpendicular.
So PT = 12, QT = 5, and angle PTQ = 90°. Use Pythagorean Theorem: PQ² = 12² + 5².

problems.question: In rectangle EFGH, diagonal EG = 3x + 7 and diagonal FH = 5x - 9. Find x and the length of each diagonal.
hints: In a rectangle, diagonals are congruent: EG = FH.
3x + 7 = 5x - 9. Solve: 16 = 2x, so x = 8. Each diagonal = 3(8) + 7 = 31.

problems.question: In parallelogram ABCD, AB = 2x + 3 and CD = 4x - 9. Also, BC = x + 8. Find x, AB, CD, and BC.
hints: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are congruent: AB = CD → 2x + 3 = 4x - 9.

scaffold.title: Proving a Quadrilateral Is a Parallelogram
scaffold.content:
So far the properties have run one direction: *if* a shape is a parallelogram, *then* its opposite sides are congruent, its opposite angles are congruent, and its diagonals bisect each other. Proofs run the other direction. You are handed a quadrilateral and some facts, and you have to decide whether those facts force it to be a parallelogram.

**The five ways to prove it.** A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if ANY ONE of these is true:
1. **Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel** — this is the definition.
2. **Both pairs of opposite sides are congruent.**
3. **Both pairs of opposite angles are congruent.**
4. **The diagonals bisect each other** (they cut each other exactly in half).
5. **One pair of opposite sides is both parallel AND congruent.**

Any single one of the five is enough. You do not need to show all of them — pick whichever matches the facts you were given, prove that one, and name it.

**Condition 5 is the efficient one.** It needs facts about only one pair of sides, where the others need facts about two pairs. If a problem hands you one pair that is both parallel and congruent, stop there.

**The trap: the two facts must describe the SAME pair.** "One pair parallel and one pair congruent" is not condition 5 unless it is the *same* pair. If PQ ∥ SR but the congruent sides are PS and QR — the other pair — you have described an isosceles trapezoid just as well as a parallelogram, so nothing is proven. Always check which sides each given fact is actually about.

**Proving it with coordinates.** When you have vertices instead of a diagram, each condition becomes arithmetic:
- **Parallel** → equal **slopes**.
- **Congruent** → equal lengths by the **distance formula**.
- **Diagonals bisect each other** → both diagonals share the same **midpoint**.

The midpoint route is often the fastest, because one midpoint calculation per diagonal settles it — no slopes, no radicals to compare.

**Finish by naming the condition.** Computing that two slopes match is not yet a proof. The proof is the computation plus the sentence "both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, so ABCD is a parallelogram by definition." The named condition is what turns arithmetic into an argument.
scaffold.initialPrompt: Here's the reversal we're about to make. You already know that in a parallelogram the diagonals bisect each other. Now flip it: if I tell you a quadrilateral's diagonals bisect each other, does it HAVE to be a parallelogram? What's your instinct?

scaffold.title: We-Do: Parallelogram Proofs — Guided Practice

problems.question: In quadrilateral ABCD, you are told that AB ∥ CD and AB = CD. Is ABCD necessarily a parallelogram? Name the theorem that justifies your answer.
problems.answer: Yes. If ONE pair of opposite sides is both parallel AND congruent, the quadrilateral is a parallelogram. Here AB and CD are opposite sides, and they are given as both parallel and congruent, so ABCD is a parallelogram. This is the most efficient of the five conditions — it needs facts about only one pair of sides instead of two.
hints: List what you are given, then check it against the five ways to prove a parallelogram. Are AB and CD opposite sides or adjacent ones?
AB and CD are opposite sides, and you have TWO facts about that same pair: parallel and congruent.
That is exactly the fifth condition — one pair of opposite sides both parallel and congruent is enough on its own.

problems.question: The diagonals of quadrilateral WXYZ meet at point M. WM = 3x - 4, MY = x + 6, XM = 2y + 1, and MZ = 5y - 8. Find x and y, and explain why WXYZ must be a parallelogram.
problems.answer: For the diagonals to bisect each other, M must be the midpoint of both. Set the halves of each diagonal equal. Diagonal WY: 3x - 4 = x + 6 → 2x = 10 → x = 5, giving WM = MY = 11. Diagonal XZ: 2y + 1 = 5y - 8 → 9 = 3y → y = 3, giving XM = MZ = 7. Both diagonals are cut into two equal pieces, so the diagonals bisect each other, and therefore WXYZ is a parallelogram.
hints: Which condition involves the diagonals meeting at a point? "Diagonals bisect each other" — meaning M is the midpoint of both.
Being the midpoint of WY means WM = MY. Set 3x - 4 = x + 6 and solve. Do the same for the other diagonal.
x = 5 and y = 3. Substitute back to confirm both halves match (11 and 11, 7 and 7), then name the condition — that verification IS the proof.

problems.question: In quadrilateral PQRS, PQ ∥ SR and PS = QR. Must PQRS be a parallelogram? Explain.
problems.answer: No. The parallel pair is PQ and SR, but the congruent pair is PS and QR — a DIFFERENT pair of sides. None of the five conditions covers that combination. An isosceles trapezoid fits this description exactly: one pair of parallel sides, and the two non-parallel legs congruent, with no second pair of parallel sides. So PQRS could be a parallelogram, but it does not have to be.
hints: Check carefully which sides each fact is about. Is the parallel pair the same pair as the congruent pair?
The fifth condition requires ONE pair that is both parallel and congruent. Here the parallel pair and the congruent pair are different pairs — so that condition does not apply.
Try to draw a counterexample: a shape with one pair of parallel sides and congruent legs. That is an isosceles trapezoid, and it is not a parallelogram.

problems.question: Quadrilateral ABCD has vertices A(-2, 1), B(3, 3), C(5, -1), and D(0, -3). Prove that ABCD is a parallelogram using coordinates.
problems.answer: Compare opposite sides. Slope of AB = (3 - 1)/(3 - (-2)) = 2/5; slope of DC = (-1 - (-3))/(5 - 0) = 2/5 — equal, so AB ∥ DC. Slope of BC = (-1 - 3)/(5 - 3) = -2; slope of AD = (-3 - 1)/(0 - (-2)) = -2 — equal, so BC ∥ AD. Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, which is the definition of a parallelogram. As a second confirmation, AB = √(5² + 2²) = √29 and DC = √29, while BC = √(2² + 4²) = 2√5 and AD = 2√5, so both pairs are congruent too. (A third route: both diagonals have midpoint (3/2, 0), so they bisect each other.)
hints: A coordinate proof turns a geometry claim into arithmetic. Pick a condition you can compute — slopes prove parallel, the distance formula proves congruent.
Find the slope of AB and the slope of DC. Careful with the order of the points on DC: going D → C keeps it as the side opposite AB.
Both come out 2/5, so AB ∥ DC. Do the same for BC and AD — both give -2. Both pairs parallel is the definition, so the proof is complete. Naming the condition at the end is what makes it a proof.

scaffold.initialPrompt: You're told a quadrilateral has AB ∥ CD and AB = CD — nothing else. Before we check the list: do you think that's enough to guarantee a parallelogram, and which pair of sides are those two?

scaffold.title: Trapezoids and Kites
scaffold.content:
**Trapezoids** have exactly one pair of parallel sides (called **bases**). The non-parallel sides are called **legs**.

**Isosceles Trapezoid** (congruent legs):
• Base angles are congruent
• Diagonals are congruent
• Legs are congruent
• Same-side angles between a base and leg are supplementary

**Midsegment of a Trapezoid:**
The segment connecting the midpoints of the legs is called the midsegment. Its length = (base₁ + base₂) / 2 (the average of the two bases).

**Kites** have two pairs of consecutive congruent sides (not opposite):
• One pair of opposite angles is congruent (between the non-equal sides)
• Diagonals are perpendicular
• One diagonal bisects the other
• Area = (d₁ × d₂) / 2
scaffold.initialPrompt: A trapezoid has bases of 8 and 14. What is the length of the midsegment? Can you see why it's called the 'average' of the bases?

scaffold.title: I-Do: Trapezoid and Kite Calculations

examples.problem: A trapezoid has bases of 14 and 22. Find the length of the midsegment.
examples.solution:
Midsegment = (base₁ + base₂) / 2 = (14 + 22) / 2 = 36 / 2 = **18**

The midsegment is always parallel to both bases and exactly halfway between them.

examples.problem: In isosceles trapezoid ABCD, ∠A = (4x + 10)° and ∠D = (8x - 10)°, where AB ∥ DC. Find x and all four angle measures.
examples.solution:
In a trapezoid with AB ∥ DC, angles A and D are same-side interior angles (supplementary):
(4x + 10) + (8x - 10) = 180
12x = 180 → x = 15

∠A = 4(15) + 10 = **70°**, ∠D = 8(15) - 10 = **110°**
Isosceles: ∠B = ∠A = **70°**, ∠C = ∠D = **110°**

Check: 70 + 70 + 110 + 110 = 360° ✓

examples.problem: Kite WXYZ has diagonals WY = 16 and XZ = 12, with the diagonals perpendicular. Find the area of the kite.
examples.solution:
Area of a kite = (d₁ × d₂) / 2
Area = (16 × 12) / 2 = 192 / 2 = **96 square units**

This works because the kite can be split into 4 right triangles by its diagonals.

problems.question: Trapezoid MNOP has bases MN = 28 and OP = 16. The midsegment measures (2x + 4). Find x and the midsegment length.
hints: Midsegment = (28 + 16) / 2 = 22.

problems.question: In isosceles trapezoid RSTU with RS ∥ UT, ∠R = 65°. Find all other angles.
hints: Isosceles trapezoid: base angles congruent → ∠S = ∠R = 65°.
Same-side interior supplementary: ∠U = 180° - 65° = 115°, ∠T = 115°. Check: 65+65+115+115=360° ✓.

In parallelogram WXYZ, WX = 3a + 5 and YZ = 5a - 7. Find a and the length of WX.
hints: Opposite sides congruent: 3a + 5 = 5a - 7. So 12 = 2a, a = 6. WX = 3(6)+5 = 23.

problems.question: Is a square always a rhombus? Is a rhombus always a square? Explain.
problems.answer: Yes, a square is always a rhombus (4 congruent sides). No, a rhombus is not always a square—it doesn't require right angles.
hints: A square has 4 congruent sides (rhombus) AND 4 right angles (rectangle). A rhombus only needs 4 congruent sides.

problems.question: A trapezoid has bases of 12 and 20. Find the midsegment length.
hints: Midsegment = (base₁ + base₂) / 2 = (12 + 20) / 2 = 16.

problems.question: A rhombus has diagonals of 30 and 16. Find the length of each side and the perimeter.
hints: Half-diagonals: 15 and 8. Side = √(15² + 8²) = √(225+64) = √289 = 17. Perimeter = 4 × 17 = 68.

answerKeys.pq-pf1: Yes — one pair of opposite sides both parallel and congruent.
answerKeys.pq-pf2: x = 5, y = 3; halves are 11/11 and 7/7, so the diagonals bisect each other.
answerKeys.pq-pf3: No — the parallel pair and the congruent pair are different pairs (isosceles trapezoid).
answerKeys.pq-pf4: Slopes: AB = DC = 2/5 and BC = AD = -2, so both pairs of opposite sides are parallel.
